questions.question: The dual of a Boolean function [latex]F(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}, +, \cdot , ' ) [/latex] , written as [latex]F^{D}[/latex], is the same expression as that of F with + and  [latex]\cdot[/latex]  swapped. F is said to be self-dual if [latex]F=F^{D}[/latex].  The number of self-dual functions with n Boolean variables is
questions.explanation:
A self-dual function satisfies [latex]F(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_n)=\overline{F(x_1,\dots,x_n)}[/latex].

The [latex]2^n[/latex] input rows form [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] complementary pairs. Choosing F on one row of a pair fixes F on the other, so we freely choose [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] bits.

Number of self-dual functions = [latex]2^{2^{n-1}}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]2^{2^{n-1}}[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: Let R1 and R2 be two 4-bit registers that store numbers in 2's complement form. For the operation R1+R2, which one of the following values of R1 and R2 gives an arithmetic overflow?
questions.explanation:
4-bit 2's complement range: [latex]-8[/latex] to [latex]+7[/latex].

- 1011 + 1110 = [latex](-5)+(-2)=-7[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits
- 1100 + 1010 = [latex](-4)+(-6)=-10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] overflow
- 0011 + 0100 = [latex]3+4=7[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits
- 1001 + 1111 = [latex](-7)+(-1)=-8[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits

Answer: R1 = 1100 and R2 = 1010

questions.question: For a Boolean variable [latex]x[/latex], which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]x\cdot1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (identity).
- [latex]x+1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x+1=1[/latex].
- [latex]x\cdot x=0[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x\cdot x=x[/latex] (idempotence).
- [latex]x+\bar{x}=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (complement).

Answer: [latex]x+1=x[/latex] and [latex]x.x=0[/latex]

In this system, two integers [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are represented as [latex]A=01010 [/latex] and [latex]B=11010 [/latex]. [latex]A=01010=+10[/latex], [latex]B=11010=-6[/latex].

- [latex]A-B=10+6=16[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] exceeds +15, overflow
- [latex]B-A=-16[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits (lowest value)
- [latex]2B=-12[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits

Answer: A [latex]-[/latex] B

questions.question:
The output of a 2-input multiplexer is connected back to one of its inputs as shown in the figure.

Match the functional equivalence of this circuit to one of the following options.
questions.explanation:
The output Q is fed back to input 0.
- S = 1: Q follows input 1 (the data input D).
- S = 0: Q = Q, so it holds its old value.

It is transparent while S = 1 and holds while S = 0, which is a level-triggered D latch (S acts as enable). There is no clock edge, so it is not a flip-flop.

Answer: D Latch

questions.question:
Consider a digital logic circuit consisting of three 2-to-1 multiplexers M1, M2, and M3 as shown below. [latex] X 1 [/latex] and [latex] X 2 [/latex] are inputs of [latex] M 1 [/latex]. [latex] X 3 [/latex] and [latex] X 4 [/latex] are inputs of [latex] M 2 [/latex]. [latex] A, B [/latex], and [latex] C [/latex] are select lines of [latex] M 1, M 2 [/latex], and [latex] M 3 [/latex], respectively.

For an instance of inputs [latex] X \mathbf{X l}=\mathbf{X} \mathbf{2}=\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{X} 3=\mathbf{0} [/latex], and [latex] \mathrm{X} 4=\mathbf{0} [/latex], the number of combinations of [latex] A, B, C [/latex] that give the output [latex] Y=1 [/latex] is _____
questions.explanation:
Look at each multiplexer separately:
- M1: both inputs [latex]X1=X2=1[/latex], so [latex]Q1=1[/latex] whatever A is.
- M2: both inputs [latex]X3=X4=0[/latex], so [latex]Q2=0[/latex] whatever B is.
- M3: [latex]Y=Q1=1[/latex] when [latex]C=0[/latex], and [latex]Y=Q2=0[/latex] when [latex]C=1[/latex].

So [latex]Y=1[/latex] exactly when [latex]C=0[/latex]; A and B are free: [latex]2\times2=4[/latex] combinations.

Answer: 4

questions.question:
Consider the following [latex]4[/latex]-variable Boolean function

[latex] F(A, B, C, D)=\Sigma m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11) [/latex]

Consider [latex]A[/latex] as MSB, [latex]D[/latex] as LSB. Which one of the following options represents the minimal sum of products form for the above function?
Note: [latex]{+}[/latex] is OR operation, [latex]{\cdot}[/latex] is AND operation, [latex]{\prime}[/latex] is NOT operation
questions.explanation:
Listing the minterms in binary (bit order [latex]A,B,C,D[/latex]): [latex]0{=}0000,\,1{=}0001,\,2{=}0010,\,3{=}0011,\,8{=}1000,\,9{=}1001,\,10{=}1010,\,11{=}1011[/latex].

In every single one of these [latex]8[/latex] minterms, the [latex]B[/latex] bit is [latex]0[/latex] — while [latex]A,C,D[/latex] each range freely over both values (covering all [latex]2\times2\times2=8[/latex] combinations). This exactly matches the full set of minterms where [latex]B=0[/latex], regardless of [latex]A,C,D[/latex].

So the function reduces to the single literal [latex]F=B'[/latex] (its minimal SOP form has just one term).

Answer: B′

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Consider a Boolean function [latex]F[/latex] with the following minterm expression:

[latex] F(P, Q, R, S)=\sum m(1,2,3,4,5,7,10,12,13,14) [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are the minimal sum-of-products expression(s) of [latex]F[/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
Plotting [latex]F(P,Q,R,S)=\sum m(1,2,3,4,5,7,10,12,13,14)[/latex] on a [latex]4[/latex]-variable K-map, the essential prime implicants are [latex]\bar P S[/latex] (covering minterms [latex]1,3,5,7[/latex]) and [latex]Q\bar R[/latex] (covering [latex]4,5,12,13[/latex]).

After these two terms, the still-uncovered minterms are [latex]2,10,14[/latex] (minterm [latex]3,4,5,12,13[/latex] already covered). These three remaining minterms can be covered in two equally minimal ways, giving two different valid minimal SOP expressions:

- Using [latex]\bar P\bar Q R[/latex] (covers [latex]2,3[/latex]) and [latex]P R\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]10,14[/latex]): [latex]F=\bar P S+Q\bar R+\bar P\bar Q R+PR\bar S[/latex].
- Using [latex]PQ\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]12,14[/latex]) and [latex]\bar Q R\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]2,10[/latex]): [latex]F=\bar P S+Q\bar R+PQ\bar S+\bar Q R\bar S[/latex].

Both use exactly [latex]4[/latex] terms and correctly cover all [latex]10[/latex] minterms with none extra, so both are valid minimal-cost solutions (this function has two equally-good minimal SOP forms because the remaining minterms admit two different but equally cheap coverings).

Answer: [latex]\bar P S+Q\bar R+\bar P\bar Q R+PR\bar S[/latex] and [latex]\bar P S+Q\bar R+PQ\bar S+\bar Q R\bar S[/latex]
